newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian Broadcasting Corp Midday Update.
newsitem.headline: Australian Broadcasting Corp Midday Update.

text.p: COSTELLO SAYS AUSTRALIA HAS COME A LONG WAY WITH RATES
The Federal Treasurer, Peter Costello, says people should look at how far interest rates have been cut already, before getting fixated on the next movement in rates.
There have been calls for another cut following yesterday's low inflation figures.
The Treasurer says the Reserve Bank will be looking at wages figures and at the longer-term economic situation in making decisions about interest rates.
Mr Costello has told ABC Radio, interest rates have already been cut by 2 per cent, with home mortgage rates now the lowest since 1969.

"These are enormous strides. People sit round and say 'can you make it better'. Well, we're always working on the fundamentals to try and get them right, but let's just remember where we were and how far we've come before we get too fixated on the next step", the Treasurer said.
COSTELLO SAYS HIS STAFF NOT INVOLVED IN LEAKED REPORT
The Federal Treasurer, Peter Costello, says his staff have not been involved in security lapses which have led to two secret documents from a South Pacific economic forum being made public.
The first document was a briefing to Mr Costello for the forum meeting held in Cairns two weeks ago.
The second, made public yesterday, was the briefing notes for bilateral meetings held following the forum.
The Treasury Secretary, Ted Evans, has commissioned the Inspector-General of Intelligence and Security, Ron McLeod, to inquire into how the confidential briefing became public.
Mr Costello has told ABC Radio, full action will be taken when the report is finished, but says no member of his staff was involved.
He says it appears there was a lapse of security at the agency level, which will be investigated by the Inspector-General of Intelligence.
AUSTRALIANS SEEKING COMPENSATION FROM BRIDGE ACCIDENT
Australian team leaders to the Maccabiah Games in Tel Aviv are seeking compensation from the Israeli Government for the two deaths and dozens of injuries in last week's bridge collapse.
The call came after a damning report from a special inquiry into the disaster, which blamed all those who designed and built the bridge.
The Inquiry's report confirmed what had been obvious for days; that substandard design and materials had produced a failure of a bridge.
A police inquiry still to be finalised is expected to follow up with criminal charges.
But the President of the Australian Jewish Maccabiah organisation, Tom Goldman, says there is another concern for those affected by the disaster - the financial burden.

Mr Goldman says Israel should lend the Australian team members half a million dollars, until insurance payments come through, hinting at surprise that Israel's Government had not already made an offer.
COOK ISLANDS ACCEPTS AUSTRALIAN APOLOGY OVER LEAKED REPORT
The Cook Islands Government says it has accepted an apology from Australia over comments contained in an Australian briefing paper about South Pacific countries.
An inquiry is underway into how two confidential papers were leaked.
The Cook Islands Prime Minister, Sir Geoffrey Henry, has discussed the first leaked paper with the Australian High Commissioner, Geoffrey Miller.
The paper included the Cook Islands and its Prime Minister in highly critical comments about South Pacific Island economies and personal habits of politicians.
Sir Geoffrey's office says the High Commissioner expressed deep regret over the paper.

The office says Sir Geoffrey rejected criticism his country's economy was in free fall, and has invited Australian specialists to visit and examine his country's economic reform. In Australia, Treasury Secretary Ted Evans has asked the Inspector General of Intelligence and Security to hold an inquiry into how the papers became public.
The Treasurer, Peter Costello, says the lapse of security happened at the Departmental level, and appropriate action will be taken after the inquiry.
HOSTAGES RELEASED BY BOUGAINVILLE REBELS
Bougainville rebels have released five members of Papua New Guinea's security force they took hostage last September.
The hostages were captured during a massacre at Kangu Beach 10 months ago.
Today, they were handed over to a senior New Zealand diplomat.
John Hayes, a former New Zealand High Commissioner to Papua New Guinea, accompanied the hostages from where they were released into his care to the Royal New Zealand Navy frigat Canterbury.
The word from the Canterbury is that all five are now safety aboard.
They are expected to arrive in Bucha Island at first light tomorrow.
The release of the hostages is a follow up to the recent peace talks between warring Bougainvillians hosted at the Burnam military base near Christchurch.
NATIONAL CRIME FIGURES RELEASED TODAY
Figures released today show a rise in most categories of crime recorded in Australia last year.
But the number of murder victims fell despite the Port Arthur tragedy.
The Bureau of Statistics says the number of murder victims recorded in Australia last year rose 4 per cent to 311.

The Northern Territory had the highest number of murder victims, calculated on the number of victims per 100,000 people, followed by Tasmania which recorded 35 deaths in a single incident at Port Arthur.
Assault, sexual assault, robbery, theft and unlawful entry were all up nationally, with crimes recorded in New South Wales accounting for the major proportion of the overall increase.
On a brighter note, the number of motor vehicle thefts fell by 3 per cent, with the biggest fall of 20 per cent in Western Australia.
-- Reuters Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
